And the nonprofit has some help: Students with the Boise Student Transitional Education Program (STEP) and Cole Valley Christian fifth graders packed boxes with turkeys, cake mix, potatoes, canned goods and other ingredients for holiday meals. Teachers and paraprofessionals regularly arrange volunteers to help them develop vocational skills, teacher Brendan Reidt told Idaho Education News. “ We’re giving back, and we’re teaching them that giving back is very rewarding,” said paraprofessional Vivien Dickens. “A nd it kind of sticks with you for the rest of your life.” Boise School District transitional education students fill boxes with ingredients for Thanksgiving meals with the Society of St. Vincent de Paul on Friday, Nov. 20, in Garden City. items.body: With a week and a half left in Medicare open enrollment, insurance brokers are encouraging Idaho seniors to read mailed notices from their insurer to understand if their plan is being canceled, and reach out for help. (Photo by Getty Images) Nearly a third of Idaho seniors who have private Medicare coverage are set to lose those health insurance plans next year. More than 60,000 Idahoans are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that are set to be canceled statewide or in their county, according to federal data analyzed by Idaho health insurance brokers. Your Health Idaho is in open enrollment. Insurance premiums hikes might be tamped down. With a week and a half left in Medicare open enrollment, insurance brokers are encouraging Idaho seniors to read mailed notices from their insurer to understand if their plan is being canceled, and reach out for help. “It’s actually causing a lot of panic with seniors,” Coeur d’Alene based broker Malia Rogers said. This year, she said seniors are navigating plan cancellations, trying to make sure their medical providers are still accepting their Medicare Advantage plan, and checking that their prescriptions are still covered. “Don’t try to do it on your own, because there’s so many things … to watch out for,” Rogers said. “My recommendation is to find a broker. Brokers have a trained set of eyes, and we never charge for our services, so our services are free.” Nearly half of the people who are on Medicare in Idaho are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, which tend to cover extra benefits than traditional Medicare. Some seniors are being hit harder by the cancellations because their Medicare Advantage plans were tailored to their needs. Marcia Benton, a broker in Meridian, said some people in North Idaho won’t be able to find comparable plans. Rural areas, she said, will also be hit hard. If your Medicare Advantage plan is being terminated, what can you do? Open enrollment for Medicare ends Dec. 7. In a statement last month, Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron encouraged Medicare members to tap free help from a licensed agent or a Medicare counselor with Senior Health Insurance Benefits Advisors, a state service available by phone at 1-800-247-4422 or online at https://doi.idaho.gov/shiba/about-shiba/ask-shiba/ . “While some carriers are exiting the market, Idaho still offers a competitive selection of plans and strong consumer protections,” Cameron said. But if your Medicare Advantage plan is being terminated, you may be able to switch to another plan or traditional Medicare after through a special enrollment period. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Insurers haven’t seen federal pay rates keep up with inflation, broker says State insurance officials say the scalebacks in Idaho and across the nation are caused by a mix of regulations, federal pay structures and rising costs. This is the second year of major Medicare Advantage cancellations in Idaho, but brokers say that less Idahoans are enrolled in plans being terminated this year than last year. Insurance carriers haven’t seen federal pay rates keep up with sharp medical inflation, Benton said. She called the Medicare Advantage market unstable and said plan closures can result in higher costs for consumers. “But we do need to stop having these closures. Because moving mass amounts of people from plan to plan is not good for any carrier,” Benton said. UnitedHealthcare is closing two Idaho plans, along with withdrawing from several counties across the state. About 16,500 Idaho seniors are enrolled in the plans affected. items.title: Former Idaho senator and insurance director to lead state Health and Welfare agency — for now
items.summary: The Pete T. Cenarrusa state office building in Boise, the longtime headquarters for Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and the Division of Medicaid. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Captial Sun) Idaho’s top insurance official and a former legislator will temporarily lead Idaho’s largest state agency, the governor announced Wednesday. Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron, right
items.body: The Pete T. Cenarrusa state office building in Boise, the longtime headquarters for Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and the Division of Medicaid. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Captial Sun) Idaho’s top insurance official and a former legislator will temporarily lead Idaho’s largest state agency, the governor announced Wednesday. Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron, right. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Department of Insurance) Idaho State Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron will serve as interim director of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare starting Nov. 30, according to a press release. Cameron had a prior stint as interim head of the health agency when a former director retired in 2024. Idaho Gov. Brad Little also appointed Weston Trexler as interim director of the Idaho Department of Insurance until Little selects a permanent Health and Welfare director after the 2027 legislative session. The session begins Jan. 11 and typically lasts about three months. Former Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron stepped down , after just over a year leading the agency. “Dean Cameron and Weston Trexler bring decades of experience, strong leadership, and a deep understanding of their respective agencies,” Little said in the press release. “Both have a proven commitment to serving Idahoans, and I have confidence in their ability to provide steady leadership during these transitions. I appreciate their willingness to step into these roles and continue the important work of delivering important services to the people of Idaho.” Trexler has served as deputy director as an actuary at the insurance department since 2019 and has been at the agency since 2012, according to the release. As interim director during the legislative session, Cameron will be tasked with working with state legislators on a proposal to restore budget cuts for disability caregivers , as outlined in the agency’s budget request for the upcoming session. The 2026 legislative session was marked by deep cuts government-wide to avoid a projected budget shortfall. Cameron has led the Department of Insurance since he was appointed by former Gov. Butch Otter in 2015. Prior to his appointment, he served in the Idaho state Senate for 25 years, during which he co-chaired the state’s powerful budget-writing committee. Health and Welfare has more than 3,000 employees and oversees public assistance programs such as Medicaid, food benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and the Women and Infant Children program, known as WIC. The agency also provides public health services, regulates long-term care facilities, runs the state’s mental health hospitals, oversees child welfare and provides services for people with developmental disabilities. The agency’s total budget is more than $5 billion of mostly federal funds. The new director will oversee a major shift to administering Idaho’s entire Medicaid program through private managed care companies , as directed by the Idaho Legislature’s House Bill 345. The full transition to managed care oversight of Medicaid is expected to happen by 2030. The Health and Welfare chief will also see the state’s administration of around $183 million in grants for the second year of the five-year federal Rural Health Transformation program. The new permanent director will be the fourth since Little took office in 2019. Prior to Charron, Alex Adams served a little over a year in the position before President Donald Trump appointed him to lead the federal Administration for Children and Families under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Adams’ predecessor, Dave Jeppesen, led the agency for five years before retiring in 2023. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.title: Post-election audit reveals flaws in Benewah County’s hand-counting system
items.summary: In Benewah County, the only thing worse than state officials coming to town is if the feds show up, Secretary of State Phil McGrane said Tuesday. The rural panhandle county was one of eight selected for a random post-election audit. Staff from McGrane’s office headed north earlier this month to canvas results and examine the county’s practices. Benewah is one of three counties that hand counts all
items.body: In Benewah County, the only thing worse than state officials coming to town is if the feds show up, Secretary of State Phil McGrane said Tuesday. The rural panhandle county was one of eight selected for a random post-election audit. Staff from McGrane’s office headed north earlier this month to canvas results and examine the county’s practices. Benewah is one of three counties that hand counts all ballots, and it was the last of all 44 counties to report results, which was completed around noon the day after the election. During the audit, McGrane’s staff found out why. “Needless to say, there are numerous things we identified,” he said. Benewah has a unique system. Instead of receiving one consolidated ballot, voters could receive up to five different sheets of colored paper ballots for the various candidates and questions. One precinct had 700 voters so poll workers, after assisting voters all day, had to hand count up to five sheets for each of those voters. The poll workers then hand tallied results into notebooks that the county workers created themselves, which McGrane said is “certainly not best practice.” Click to view slideshow. “Ours are developed based on national standards,” McGrane said of the tally notebooks. Then, after auditing the results, state workers found none of the numbers matched up. The number of ballots reported, the number of ballots audited and the number of voters were all different. In addition to having a unique system as a county, the audit team found “inconsistencies” between each precinct. McGrane said the audit highlights the challenges of hand counting. This year’s long ballot with multiple races and voter initiatives was a stress test for Benewah’s election system — and a chance to make improvements. “We’re going to be taking the overt step of going back and working with them on some of their practices, and … looking at are there other ways because there is a point where this just becomes too complicated,” McGrane said. While local officials in Saint Maries were at first hesitant to deal with state employees coming in from Boise, McGrane said they eventually saw an opportunity for help. “They welcome it,” he said. The report on Benewah County on Tuesday was part of a State Board of Canvassers meeting. McGrane, along with State Controller Brandon Woolf and State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth, certified the Nov. 3 general election, finalizing the results of all local, state and federal races in Idaho. The results are now official. The State Board of Canvassers certified the results of the general election on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, at the Capitol in Boise. The board is made up of State Controller Brandon Woolf, Secretary of State Phil McGrane and State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth. items.summary: Updated Wednesday, Nov. 25, with a statement from Durst and clarification that current school leaders and the charter commission have not shared information or documentation with EdNews showing that Durst committed wrongdoing or was forced to leave the school. Branden Durst, a former Idaho lawmaker whose education endeavors have drawn scrutiny over the years, is no longer employed at the sports-fo
items.body: Updated Wednesday, Nov. 25, with a statement from Durst and clarification that current school leaders and the charter commission have not shared information or documentation with EdNews showing that Durst committed wrongdoing or was forced to leave the school. Branden Durst, a former Idaho lawmaker whose education endeavors have drawn scrutiny over the years, is no longer employed at the sports-focused charter school he opened earlier this year. Durst’s departure comes less than six months after Brabeion Academy opened in Nampa. The Idaho Public Charter School Commission is also investigating reports of financial irregularities at the school, commission executive director Rachel Burk said Tuesday. Durst left Brabeion on Oct. 30, according to a separation and transition agreement EdNews obtained Tuesday through a public records request. In a phone call the with EdNews the morning after this story was published, Durst confirmed that he is leaving the school and denied any connection between his departure and the commission’s investigation. Durst, who is still listed on the school’s website as founder and CEO, stressed that he is not a signatory on any transactions at the school. He accused EdNews of “malice” and threatened a lawsuit for reporting of his departure and the commission’s investigation. The commission and current school leaders have not shared information or documentation with EdNews showing that Durst committed wrongdoing or was forced to leave the school. “I left voluntarily,” he told Ednews. His departure from various roles at both the school and its founding nonprofit, including chief strategy and innovation officer and CEO, was set to be announced on Dec. 31, according to the agreement. Durst will be paid his monthly salary of $8,333 from Brabeion Academy through the end of the year. He also received more than $40,000 in delayed compensation for work he did before the school opened in August. Burk said a former treasurer at the school reported financial irregularities to the charter commission, which her staff is investigating. Meeting minutes show Tom Moore resigned as treasurer and vice chair of the board on Aug. 25, days before school started. Commission staff is awaiting more information from the school, Burk said, before presenting investigation findings to commissioners at their December meeting. On Wednesday, Brabeion’s Board of Directors reaffirmed “its unwavering commitment to doing what is best for our students, parents, teachers, and staff,” in a news release. Trustees said they have complied with requests for information from the charter commission and are committed to financial transparency. “Brabeion Academy is bigger than any one individual,” the statement reads. “Our mission, our students and our commitment to educational excellence remain our highest priorities.” The board made the right decision to sever ties with Durst to save the school, Moore told EdNews Tuesday. “Branden Durst will do what’s in his self-serving interest before the school,” he said. Previously, Durst was at the center of a number of controversies in the West Bonner School District, where he served briefly as superintendent. Part of that issue centered on his inability to secure a certificate to qualify for the position. The saga ended earlier this year with a legal settlement. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at the Calvary Baptist Church in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) About two-thirds of Idaho’s more than 1 million registered voters cast ballots in the midterm election held earlier this month, according to finalized state election data. The turnout didn’t eclipse rates from 2018, when the governor seat was open without an incumbent, but this year’s election still turned out to be the state’s largest midterm election, with about 734,000 voters showing up, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said Tuesday. McGrane, the state’s top election official, attributes that last metric to the state’s years as one of the nation’s fastest growing states. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican, attends a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “It really was a successful election,” McGrane said. “When you think about 734,000 people going through and doing the same thing. That’s a huge Herculean effort.” Weeks after the Nov. 3 general election, the Idaho State Board of Canvassers on Tuesday certified the results of the election as official. At the board’s meeting at the Idaho State Capitol, officials delved into the results of audits of counties’ election results — including in two counties that underreported votes — and reflected on lessons learned from the election. The final results showed that no races in Idaho were close enough to warrant a free recount, McGrane said. But he said there still might be a recount in a county assessor race in Shoshone County. Here’s a few snapshots about how voters turned out to vote earlier this month: About 40% of voters didn’t cast ballots at the polls on Election Day. About half of those votes were early in person, for a total of roughly 146,000, and the other half were by absentee ballot, for a total of roughly 145,000. Both of those voting types are becoming more popular, McGrane said. Overall, the rate of voters who turned out this year was close to matching the 2018 election, which saw the highest turnout of a midterm election in recent years when nearly 67% of registered voters cast ballots. But this year’s turnout still pales in comparison to years when the president is on the ballot, when an average of nearly 76% of voters show up. About 56,000 Idahoans registered to vote on Election Day. McGrane said that might’ve contributed to lines at polling places in some areas. Registering to vote typically takes longer than checking in at the polls. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s top election official addressed issues in three counties In North Idaho’s Latah County, where officials announced 2,300 unreported ballots almost a week after the election, McGrane attributed the issue to human error. The ballots had been counted on a machine, he said, but that machine’s memory device was mistakenly not uploaded to a computer that can share votes to the state’s election results. Idaho voters turned out at high rates to vote in midterm election. Some waited hours to vote. When his team flew up the day after the unreported ballots were announced to oversee a full recount, he said the room started out packed with observers. By the end of the day, the crowd had winnowed, he said. A week later, when McGrane’s team flew up again to randomly audit batches of votes in the county, he said no one showed up. “… I think we satisfied the concerns and addressed the questions on the first go around,” McGrane said. “But we will be working with them both in terms of training, and I think there’s a lot of lessons learned from their team from this, to say the least.” In eastern Idaho’s Bannock County, local election officials found 333 uncounted ballots a week after the election. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters) Ada County Democrats are calling for a change in U.S. Senate party leadership. The county party committee passed a resolution Monday to call on U.S. Senate Democrats to back U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland over New York’s U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer as majority leader. A spokesperson the statewide Idaho Democratic Party said the central committee “hasn’t had any discussion” about the potential majority leader. Schumer has been in the Senate since 1998 and was first selected as majority leader in 2021. Van Hollen was first elected in 2016, and announced on Nov. 12 he was challenging Schumer for the leadership position. “This is the first contested race for a Democratic leader in decades, and it’s an opportunity to show the country a new direction,” Ada County Democratic Party Chair Jared DeLoof said in a press release. “The leadership of the past has not been adequate to meet the challenges working families are facing. We are in a crisis. The middle class is disappearing, the wealthy hoard money at the top while the rest of us scrape by. Artificial intelligence threatens the jobs we all depend on, all while corruption goes unchecked in Washington. We need major action now on AI, health care, inflation and jobs, and Senator Van Hollen has shown he will fight for it.” During the Nov. 3 general election, Democrats flipped nine seats in the U.S. Senate and will have a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January. Members of the party that controls the chamber select their majority leader, who sets the schedule for floor business each day and serves as a spokesperson for their party’s interests. The Ada County Democrats’ resolution was sent to Schumer, Van Hollen and members of the U.S. Senate Democratic Caucus. Both of Idaho’s senators are Republican and will not be selecting the majority leader. The trust, which collapsed this year after managers set rates below their actuary’s recommendation two years in a row and is now under the control of the Idaho Department of Insurance, will continue to exist until all member schools pay off their share of a $13 million loan from Blue Cross of Idaho, which was needed to cover unpaid claims. The trust had approximately 108 member school districts, charters and education-related organizations last year, covering about 16,600 teachers, staff members and dependents. items.body: Emi Wilkes knows how important a sense of belonging is for a student. When she became a mother during her sophomore year, support from an educator at Bear Lake High helped her eventually thrive. Now as a teacher at the southeast Idaho School, she supports her own students — and uses a partnership with another teacher to expand that support. For years, Wilkes and colleague Angie Hunter have blended coursework to turn student projects into lessons in creativity, collaboration and acceptance. The teachers wanted to think outside the box with their electives: creative writing and drawing. So they started collaborating and pushing their students to do the same. The result wasn’t just captivating poems and beautiful art but a place where students feel safe, challenged and respected. “We have a lot of creative kids, but without those two they don’t have that outlet,” said Cameron Crane, Bear Lake High counselor. Passing the baton, impacting students Wilkes, 30, became a teacher because of a school counselor at Bear Lake. Wilkes was a star student in high school. Then she got pregnant her sophomore year. A guidance counselor pushed her to transfer to the alternative school. “It just kind of felt like she was trying to punish me for my mistakes,” Wilkes said. Crane, also a guidance counselor at the school at the time, stepped in. Previous administrators were “just trying to shun her to the dark woods,” Crane said. “And I’m like, ‘This is one of our brightest kids,’” Crane said. “We’re not giving up on your life because you’re pregnant — that’s insane.” Wilkes had her baby, graduated high school a year early and earned her teaching degree. She returned to Bear Lake to ensure other students with difficult life circumstances can thrive like she has. “When students are going through a hard time, I can relate so much,” Wilkes said. “I try to use my personal experiences as a ‘You can get through hard things if you put your mind to it.’” Crane said he didn’t think much of supporting Wilkes until she came back to teach at the high school where he still works. “You never know the impact you have on people,” Crane said. Now, Crane watches Wilkes influence students daily. “She has had so much impact in our valley,” he said. “I don’t think she recognizes the impact.” Creativity and collaboration Now in her sixth year as a teacher, Wilkes formed a special bond with Hunter, 47, who was her Spanish teacher growing up. Wilkes teaches English, art history and drawing. Hunter teaches Spanish, creative writing and English. The pair started collaborating three years ago in their creative writing and drawing classes. One class writes poems, then the second class illustrates them. The project has taken different forms over the years. Most recently, students illustrated an emotion, then other students wrote about the drawing without knowing what the emotion was. Click to view slideshow. For the project to work, both teachers focus on creating a culture of safety and open-mindedness in their classrooms, so students feel comfortable having their work discussed. “We respect creativity for what it is,” Hunter said. “Be yourself, be unique, be you.” A recent student was an excellent horror writer; Hunter was pleased at how respectful other students were about an unfamiliar genre. “It might not be for them. It might not be what they read, but they were able to have that admiration and respect,” Hunter said. “It was amazing.” Crane wasn’t sure it would all catch on after the first collaboration, but about 15 students signed up for each class. The next trimester, Crane had to add an extra section because so many students wanted in. Now, Crane struggles to fit more traditional English classes into the teachers’ schedules. “These two just fascinate me. What they come up with is unreal,” he said. “No judgment in either one of their classes; you can create whatever you want.” Crane remembers one student with severe disabilities who struggled in more traditional classes.

The projected $688.3 million ending balance is an increase of almost $540 million compared to the ending balance Idaho state legislators estimated at the end of the 2026 legislative session. “Things are looking positive,” said Sen. Idaho state legislators will begin working on setting the fiscal year 2028 budget once the new legislative session begins in January. So far, this year’s revenue increases are a change compared to last year, when state legislators approved across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies and departments to pay for tax changes included in the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Grow’s committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, or JFAC, is responsible for setting the state budget, which is then sent to the full Idaho House of Representatives and Idaho Senate for approval. Grow said increased revenues could create new challenges for legislators during the upcoming legislative session. “The challenge we have is when revenues look a little stronger, some may want to go back and undo the cuts, refill or replace the cuts that were made last session,” Grow said. “I’ve been told before that when things are tight, it is more a little more understandable by departments and agencies that things are tight,” Grow said. “But when revenue seems to be strong, then we get a lot of (funding) requests.” Grow said he doesn’t think the JFAC and the Idaho Legislature will reverse or backfill all of last year’s budget cuts this year. items.body: The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs medical campus in Rapid City, South Dakota. (Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight) WASHINGTON — Many military veterans are opposing a U.S. House-passed proposal to revamp retirement and disability benefits, saying it threatens future veterans’ compensation. The House passed two bills last week that address the issue. What’s at stake is whether some 58,000 — and counting — medically retired veterans who suffered combat-related injuries before meeting 20 years of service can receive both full disability and full retirement, and who pays for it. Under current law those medically retired before reaching the 20-year mark do not receive full retirement. The standalone Major Richard Star Act, which would provide full disability and retirement benefits to veterans who were injured in combat before reaching 20 years of service, passed Nov. 12 in an overwhelming 392-18 vote . The other measure, a package that combined 60 pieces of veterans-related legislation, passed by voice vote a day earlier, on Veterans Day. That package, titled the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, or TCAVA, includes the Major Richard Star Act. While the Major Richard Star Act contains no provision for funding the benefits increase, the TCAVA does in the form of cutting future disability support for sleep apnea and tinnitus, as well as raising funding fees on VA home loans. Sleep apnea and tinnitus are common injuries among veterans who are exposed to repeated loud noises and poor sleep conditions. Tinnitus, or persistent ringing and buzzing when no sound is present, ranked first among all disability compensation recipients in 2025, according to the Veteran Benefits Administration’s annual report . The TCAVA also combines dozens of provisions meant to streamline some VA infrastructure and health professional credentialing, as well as expand benefits for caregivers and survivors, including allowing survivors who remarry before age 55 to continue to be eligible for benefits, among other measures. The Major Richard Star Act would cost $13 billion over the next decade, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. The budget office does not have an estimate for TCAVA. The Senate is only in session for four more weeks in the 119th Congress, and it’s unclear if the Republican-led Senate will take up either bill for a vote. An aide in the office of Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said leadership does not have an update on the bills at this time. Future cuts? Several veterans have spoken out against TCAVA, expressing concern that future veterans will have to pay for retirement and disability benefits that current veterans should be entitled to in full. “That’s a problem I have, and my daughter just joined the Marines recently. If that passes, that takes away possible disability benefits from her in the future, if something were to happen to her,” combat U.S. Army veteran Matt Inscho, 44, told States Newsroom in an interview Thursday. Inscho, who lives in Indiana, Pennsylvania, deployed twice to Afghanistan and Iraq over six-and-a-half years until he medically retired after suffering migraines and blackouts. His main duties included repairing military aircraft. States Newsroom received numerous emails from veterans unhappy with the TCAVA. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two Idaho lawmakers from Ada County are teaming up to introduce a bill to regulate high powered e-motorbikes, citing an uptick injuries. State Rep. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two Idaho lawmakers from Ada County are teaming up to introduce a bill to regulate high powered e-motorbikes, citing an uptick injuries. State Rep. Brooke Green, D-Boise, chats with fellow legislators on the House floor on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Rep. Brooke Green, a Boise Democrat, and Sen. Treg Bernt, a Meridian Republican, on Thursday announced they plan to introduce a bill during the upcoming legislative session to require so-called e-motos — which they say can reach over 30 mph but are often marketed as e-bikes — to be classified as motorcycles. That change would require riders of e-motos to have a driver’s license with a motorcycle endorsement to ride on public roads, and for the vehicles to meet certain requirements to be considered street legal, the lawmakers say. Since the start of the year, Idaho emergency rooms have seen nearly 1,900 visits due to electric mobility devices, a category that also includes e-bikes and e-scooters, according to data from the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Young boys, between the ages of 11 and 15, accounted for 306 of the visits — the most of any demographic reported. An Idaho Statesman report published earlier Thursday highlighted the spike in injuries . Sen. Treg Bernt, R-Meridian, speaks from the Senate floor on Jan. 13, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Families are spending thousands of dollars on what they believe are bicycles, without realizing their 14-year-old cannot legally ride them down Eagle Road or on the Greenbelt,” Bernt and Green said in a joint statement. “Kids are getting seriously hurt, and we need to address this before more injuries occur.” Ahead of the holiday season, the lawmakers urged parents to not buy e-motos for children who can’t legally drive motorcycles on public roads. The proposed statewide change seems similar to an action the city of Boise took earlier this year. Other cities have taken notice, too. Meridian in July launched an education campaign focused on the use of e-bikes and e-motorcycles, BoiseDev reported. Nampa in September passed an ordinance adding local regulations, including barring e-motos from sidewalks and greenbelts if they can reach speeds in excess of 28 miles per hour, the Idaho Statesman reported. “There’s nothing wrong with enjoying these vehicles in the desert or on our public lands where motorized recreation is permitted, but motorcycles do not belong on the Greenbelt, sidewalks, or other pedestrian spaces,” the lawmakers added. “We want parents to have the facts before making expensive holiday purchases, and we’re working on bipartisan legislation to establish clear rules that keep our communities safe.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: Idaho nonprofit Envision helps provide eye exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. (Photo by Getty Images) Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision , figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss. Jay Lugo is the executive director of Envision, an Idaho 501(c)(3) nonprofit that receives hundreds of inquires a month about help with vision care and eye exams. (Photo courtesy of Envision) Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way. “I’ve seen people break down and cry when they put on a pair of glasses and discover they are able to see,” Lugo says. “It fills my heart with joy being able to do that – and I sleep well at night knowing that we are making a difference. But it’s not just me. It’s the volunteers and office co-workers who see that happen, and the 1,400 Lions Club members throughout the state who get information about what’s being done. So, a lot of people are involved.” And Lance Grady of Boise is glad for that. He didn’t break down in tears when he recently was fitted with glasses, but he did look across a street and see a squirrel climbing a tree. And he could see letters, numbers and names on buildings. “I wouldn’t have been able to see any of that without my glasses,” he said. “This has been life changing. I can drive and do other things that I was unable to do.” Grady’s story began by word of mouth. “A family friend talked with me about reaching out to the Lions,” he said. “They were determined to help me find something – without spending $400 for a pair of glasses. “I’m so thankful … a lot of stress has been lifted from me.” Lugo has seen similar stories play out many times. “When people are able to see, they can get a driver’s license, fill out a job application and be productive,” Lugo says. “There is such a big gap with healthcare, and we’re only talking about eyesight and hearing. The state doesn’t provide aid with eyeglasses for those over the age of 18, so you are not going to get eyecare assistance if you are at the poverty level.” Envision helps fill the void, providing exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. Envision offers free vision clinics for those at, or below, the poverty levels, and Lugo says demand is high. “I get at least 20 applications in my email box every day, which is about 600 a month,” he says. “Every one of those are from people who need glasses and are at the poverty level. There are a lot of people who are hurting.” Envision started in 1969 as Idaho’s only eye bank and arranging corneal transplants remain a big part of the nonprofit’s operation – along with the tradition of collecting and refurbishing used eyeglasses. People throughout the state can drop off glasses at the Division of Motor Vehicles, Walmart opticals and local optometry offices. “It’s important to note that November is National Donate Eye Month,” Lugo says. “As I’ve seen first-hand, Idaho is a giving state with the nation’s largest registry per capita. Idaho is at 62 percent, and the national average is around 38 percent.” Envision has opened a retail operation that is available to people throughout Idaho. “This gives us a sustainable source of revenue, beyond grants,” he said. “People still will get glasses at a free or discounted rate, but we’ll be able to provide something else. All people need to do is download a prescription and we can ship directly to those living in Idaho, or the United States.” Donations – large and small — will continue to be crucial to Envision’s success. items.body: House Speaker Mike Moyle, standing at right, speaks to the 2026 Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state legislator pay will be frozen in place at $25,000 for the next year, in line with state employees who did not get a pay increase from legislators this year. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Then, starting Dec. 1, 2027, the annual base pay for legislators is set to increase by about 6.7%, up to $26,685. Members of the 2026 Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation voted 5-1 to approve holding legislative pay flat for one year and then increasing it next year. House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, had recommended increasing the base pay to $26,685 starting Dec. 1 of this year, but the committee held pay flat this year after committee members Tom Harris and Bryan Mooney pointed out that state employee pay was held flat this year. “I have that in the back of my mind for the citizens and other state employees that didn’t get a raise, and I think it sends the right message if they didn’t get a raise,” Mooney said Thursday. In addition to the base pay, an unstructured constituent services allowance all legislators receive will increase to a flat $6,000. Most legislators previously received $2,500 per year in constituent services allowance, although legislators who live in geographically large legislative districts received up to $5,300. Moving forward, there will be no distinction between district sizes. Under the Idaho Constitution, state legislators do not have the power to set their own pay. Instead, the six-member Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation is responsible for setting legislator pay and benefits. The committee is made up of three appointees from the governor and three appointees from the Idaho Supreme Court. None of the committee members may hold a public office that is compensated with pay, according to the Idaho Constitution. The Idaho Legislature is not in session, but will be soon. The 2027 legislative session begins Jan. 11 at the Idaho State Capitol. Before that, the Idaho Legislature will convene for the organizational session in early December. Idaho legislators pay is set to go up, while state employees have gone without a raise Since 2024, the pay raises given to state legislators have been significantly larger than the raises for regular state employees, which are set by the Idaho Legislature. In 2024, the last time state legislators received a pay increase, the Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation approved a 25% increase in legislative pay, from $19,913 a year to $25,000 per year. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US Meanwhile, state employees have not received any pay increase since 2025 as the Idaho Legislature prioritized cutting state budgets and expenses during the 2026 legislative session to pay for costs of conforming to the tax changes in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The last time state employees received a pay increase in 2025, legislators approved raises ranging from $1.05 per hour to $1.55 per hour, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. The percentage of pay increase was different for each employee depending on their salary, but for many state employees the pay increase was less than 3%. In 2024, legislators signed off on raises of up to 3% for state employees. Many state legislators have careers, businesses and incomes outside of their legislative service. But for Idaho’s more than 20,000 state employees, their job and their pay is their livelihood. Moyle, the speaker of the Idaho House, told the Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation that state legislators will increase pay for state employees next year. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. Hospitals leaders who got awards say they'll make a big difference. Some smaller facilities who didn't get any funds say navigating the program was difficult without dedicated staff. (Getty Images) After Idaho health officials had to “sprint” to award all of its nearly $186 million federal rural health care grants, a number of small health providers say they were left without answers about why their applications were denied. Juliet Charron was named director of the Department of Health and Welfare in September 2025. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare) Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron met with state legislators on the Rural Health Transformation Committee and healthcare providers and stakeholders on the Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force in two separate meetings on Thursday in Boise. The Rural Health Transformation Program was created through the $50 billion Congress approved in July 2025 through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which also reduced an estimated nearly $1 trillion over 10 years in Medicaid spending nationwide. Idaho received about $186 million in the first year, and federal authorities announced on Nov. 9 the Gem State would receive nearly $183 million in year two. Charron said staff are trying to determine why the state received less in the second year. More than $103.5 million of Idaho’s grants in the first year were awarded to hospitals and clinics for infrastructure projects, equipment and technology upgrades in rural hospitals. “The (electronic health record software), this is transformative for us. This is something that for us to do on our own, would take almost all our cash on reserves,” said Brad Turpen, CEO, Valor Health. Valor Health, in Emmett, received two awards, totaling more than $5.4 million for a new electronic health record system that will connect to larger hospitals in the area, and new imaging equipment. John Hennessy, CEO, Bonner General, said his hospital will be able to expand its surgical capacity by adding four new suites. The 25-bed hospital is the only hospital in the county, he said, and its operating room was at full capacity. “A lot of our patients either have to wait long extended periods of time to get their surgeries done, or they end up traveling outside the area to get those procedures,” he said. He said the volume of surgeries is expected to increase 23% in the first year with the new space that will be added. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: The debate over expanding (or killing) Idaho’s private school tax credit entered a new stage Friday — when the Idaho State Tax Commission released a damning and detailed trove of data on the $50 million program. The commission report handed a lot of ammunition to opponents of the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit. The critics probably don’t have the political juice to repeal the program. However, they have some new and hard numbers on their side. The tax credits largely benefitted wealthier families. The average adjusted gross income for tax credit recipients came in at $178,000. The credits largely benefitted families who were already outside the public school system. Only 25% of the tax credits supported students who had ever attended a public school — suggesting that a lot of money went to parents who were already homeschooling their children, or sending their kids to private school. The credits largely benefitted families in urban and suburban Idaho. The Tax Commission ranked applications by legislative district (and remember, legislative districts are drawn up to have more or less the same populations). Six of the top 10 districts are in Ada or Canyon counties; two more take in pieces of Kootenai County. These three data points are crucial. They tie straight into the debate over the tax credits — which became law in 2025, with the passage of House Bill 93 . Supporters said the $5,000 to $7,500 credits would open education options to families who could not otherwise afford to leave the public school system. The credits, they said, were about providing access and supporting choice. When the Tax Commission data came out Friday — and supporters and opponents alike went straight into the spin cycle — the advocates latched onto numbers supporting their version of the narrative. They pointed to Tax Commission numbers from May : About 45% of tax credit recipients had household incomes at or below 300% of the federal poverty level (now $99,000 a year for a family of four ). In a kind of glass-quarter-full argument, the pro-tax credit Mountain States Policy Center said Friday, “3,092 awarded students — 25.3% — had previously attended public school.” Mountain States also pointed out that the tax credits made their way into households in each of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. “The data is even more surprising given that opponents claimed there were no choice options available in rural areas,” wrote Chris Cargill, Mountain States’ president, in a Sunday post defending the tax credit and criticizing news coverage of the Tax Commission’s data drop. This is all factually accurate. Some lower-income families took advantage of the credit. Some used the money to move their children out of public schools. Some explored learning options in rural communities with limited private school options. Any of the above. All of the above. However, statistics don’t just show the exceptions to the rule. They also lay out the contours of the rule itself. So, yes, residents of legislative District 34, Madison County, collected a little more than $200,000 in tax credits. But at the same time, residents in District 20, in and around Meridian, collected close to $3.6 million. Madison County is the exception. Meridian is the rule, along with similar urban and suburban districts. The Tax Commission presented a statistical aggregate. The prototypical tax credit recipients live in a six-figure household, most likely reside in or near a population center, and quite possibly they had their kids in private school long before House Bill 93 came along. That’s the prototype. And it’s an inconvenient one for supporters of the program. Which leads us to the 2027 legislative session. Saying the Tax Commission’s numbers illustrate a “rousing success,” Mountain States pounded away at expansion last week . items.body: The entrance to the hearing room for the Idaho Senate's State Affairs, Resources and Environment, and Education committees as seen on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) After months of waiting, last week the Idaho State Tax Commission finally released information about which parents are receiving the $50 million in voucher money. Idaho parents who got new private tax credit earned average of $178,000 per year, report shows Surprise, surprise, the Tax Commission report says most of the money is going to families that earn more than double the income of the average Idahoan and students who have never attended public schools. The average family that received voucher money this year earned $178,000, more than double the $84,234 of the average Idaho family. This makes the voucher program a government handout for families who can already afford to send their kids to private schools. Moreover, 75 percent of the families who took the money have never had their kids enrolled in a public school, even though advocates for the program promised that it would help students leave so-called “failing public schools” to attend private ones. And of the 25 percent of families whose kids did attend a public school, only 4.6 percent were enrolled for an entire school year a year ago. Critics of the voucher program warned that it would mainly benefit families living in urban areas rather than in rural communities. As expected, two thirds of the voucher money went to families living in just three counties – Ada, Canyon, and Kootenai. Furthermore, nearly 25 percent of the money went to only five private schools, most of them religious schools: Bishop Kelly High School in Boise, Cole Valley Christian in Meridian, Nampa Christian School, The Ambrose School in Meridian and Logos Classical Christian School in Moscow, which is led by Christian Nationalist Doug Wilson. Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, D-Boise, speaks during a Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 13, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, a retired teacher, was one of the leading opponents of the voucher program and on Friday reacted to the Tax Commission report: “It’s hard enough for working parents to make ends meet without being asked to subsidize private school tuition for families who are better off than they are.” Ward-Engelking said someone should “explain to a rural parent why their child’s school can’t afford another teacher, but the state can afford to help a well-off family pay private school tuition. That’s a pretty lousy deal for rural Idaho.” Nothing in this report should be a surprise to Gov. Brad Little or the legislators who voted to create the voucher program. They were warned that voucher programs across the country benefit the rich, and families that never sent their kids to public schools, and urban families over rural families. Still, Republican legislators, most of them rural, voted for vouchers and Gov. Little signed it into law, even though 32,000 Idahoans contacted his office and asked him to veto the bill. Vouchers, which are unpopular among most citizens, was one of the major issues in the country during the recent mid-term election. The issue contributed to the election of Democratic governors and legislators in many Republican states which adopted vouchers. In Texas, longtime Republican Gov. items.body: Idaho can tap into several existing revenue sources — and a few new sources — to compete in a changing college athletics landscape. That’s the takeaway from a gubernatorial working group, which spent the summer and fall looking at Idaho college athletics. Its work product, an eight-page report , went public Wednesday. “Do we want to compete on the national stage? If the answer is yes, no single proposal in this report will be enough,” group chair Cortney Liddiard, an Idaho Falls businessman, wrote in the report. “Idaho needs Idaho solutions, pursued together.” The report outlined the group’s proposals — albeit in general terms: Three existing funding sources could boost athletic coffers: interest earned on tuition and fee payments; withdrawals from the Higher Education Stabilization Fund, a state budget reserve; and a streamlined process for approving capital projects in athletics. Four new revenue streams also could be on the table: state lottery proceeds; a “transaction fee” on sports prediction markets; revenue streams from existing, university-owned properties; and state and local legislation to allow athletic programs “to benefit from the economic activity they generate.” The report affixes no dollar figures to any of these revenue sources. And the available money could vary widely. For example, state lottery proceeds are already spoken for; this year’s record $90 million payouts went to public schools and building projects. The stabilization fund, meanwhile, is a standalone fund dedicated solely to colleges and universities, with about $25.6 million in hand. While Wednesday’s report was short on specifics, it conveyed a sense of urgency. A battery of court cases could reshape the college sports landscape. Meanwhile, Congress is considering a far-reaching bill that would reshape college athletics; it has passed the Senate but is stalled in the House. “For these reasons, Idaho’s approach must remain flexible,” the report said. Closer to home, the State Board of Education has given Boise State University the go-ahead to cover an athletics shortfall of up to $18 million — with much of the deficit spending going to “revenue sharing” payments to Boise State athletes. “That was a prudent bridge, but it is not a practice that can or should be repeated,” Liddiard wrote. “Absent meaningful action, the board will have little choice but to require the department to eliminate that deficit, with consequences that would profoundly diminish Boise State’s ability to compete.” In a news release Wednesday, Boise State President David Hahn commended the working group. “We are carefully reviewing the report and look forward to working with the governor, Legislature, State Board and our fellow institutions to identify a path forward that strengthens college athletics across Idaho.” On Wednesday, Gov. Brad Little called the report a strong starting point. “College athletics matter to Idaho,” Little said in a news release. “They bring our communities together, carry our state’s name across the country, and help attract the students and talent our economy needs.”

items.body: When Alan Pesky’s son Lee was in the fourth grade, Alan was called in to see the headmaster. Lee was, supposedly, underperforming and acting out. The headmaster recommended that Lee would fare better in a different school. Alan got the message: “That was shorthand for he’s not very smart. The words at that time, back in the early 70s, were that the child is dumb,” he said. But Alan knew Lee was not dumb. “On the contrary — he was curious and intelligent; he just didn’t fit neatly into the picture of the school’s typical student,” Alan wrote in his memoir, “More to Life than More.” It was eventually determined that Lee had learning disabilities, but in the 70s and 80s, the diagnosis was fairly new. Alan and his wife, Wendy, struggled with finding their son the correct resources to help him. “When Lee was a child, the words “learning disability” weren’t even in the English language,” Alan said. “We didn’t have knowledge at that time of what special education and learning disabilities were all about.” Alan struggled to understand his son for many years. He said he had a hard time grasping Lee’s disabilities, which led to friction in their relationship. Sadly, in 1995, when Lee was 30, he died from a cancerous brain tumor. The loss profoundly changed Alan, and to honor his son, he was devoted to advancing research and resources for other kids like Lee. In 1997, Alan and Wendy founded the Lee Pesky Learning Center (LPLC) in Boise. “[My dad] and my mom started the Lee Pesky Center at probably the toughest times in both their lives,” said Greg Pesky, Alan and Wendy’s youngest son. “They had this crazy idea of how we could memorialize Lee … and they came up with the Pesky Center.” What started as a place for kids with dyslexia to receive tutoring has turned into a holistic approach to understanding and aiding students, families and teachers with special education resources. The programming has served at least 100,000 students and 7,000 teachers in every Idaho county over the years. Now, less than a month away from 93, Alan travels across the country, splitting his time between New York and Idaho. Although he is retired, he is still deeply involved with Lee Pesky Learning Center. “In fact, yesterday I was on a meeting for two hours with the Lee Pesky Learning Center,” Alan said. “What happens with the Lee Pesky Learning Center, and the impact that this organization can still have in the future is something that continues to excite me at my ripe old age of 93.” Alan reflects on how a place like the Lee Pesky Learning Center could have helped his family. “It would have made an enormous difference in Lee’s life,” Alan said. Despite Lee’s hardships, he graduated from Lafayette College in Pennsylvania in 1987 and became an entrepreneur. Lee co-founded The Buckin’ Bagel, a Bagel shop with multiple locations in the Boise area in the ‘90s. “If Lee were here, I would put my arms around him, give him a hug and say to him, I may have been a little difficult during your early years, but I have so much pride in how much you have achieved,” Alan said. items.body: Former students at Boise’s Timberline High School have filed a federal lawsuit, saying they were unfairly expelled amidst a public outcry over threatening online comments. The comments on the Snapchat social media platform — a graphic thread that discussed raping and killing a female student — were “crude and distasteful,” the former Timberline football players’ attorneys acknowledge in the lawsuit. But the thread was not “a serious expression of an intent to commit violence,” according to the lawsuit. Meanwhile, the attorneys said, district leaders had already publicly condemned the online comments, promising to bring the students to justice. “Plaintiffs were denied a meaningful opportunity to present their defenses to the allegations before the decision was made to punish them,” according to the lawsuit, filed Nov. 6 in U.S. District Court in Boise. The lawsuit came barely a month after the content of the social media thread went public — prompting an Oct. 3 online petition calling for immediate disciplinary action and an Oct. 7 student walkout at Timberline. Before the walkout, district officials canceled or postponed Homecoming activities at Timberline, saying the firestorm over the online thread posed a threat to safety. The lawsuit says district and school officials quickly suspended the four players involved in the “Gameday lunch” Snapchat thread. The suspensions stretched for 17 days, and according to the lawsuit, the players were not given a chance to be heard. Near the end of the 17-day suspensions, according to the lawsuit, Timberline Principal Chad Wright recommended removing the students from school, assigning them to Boise Alternative to Suspension and Expulsion school or Boise Online School for fall semester, or the remainder of the year. Three of the four students are assigned to online school for the semester or the school year, and a fourth is under a tutoring plan. The district held hearings before permanently removing the students from Timberline, the lawsuit said, but the students were not given adequate time to prepare a defense. Ultimately, the students were reassigned not because of their online comments but because of “the public’s reaction to those communications and the disruption it caused,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit does not identify the students by name — only as John Does Nos. 1 through 4. One plaintiff, identified only as Jane Roe, is the legal guardian of John Doe No. 4. The lawsuit names five Boise school administrators as defendants: Superintendent Wendy Johnson; Deputy Superintendent Nick Smith; Shelley Bonds, the area director for Timberline and neighboring schools; Jason Hutchinson, the Borah area director who oversaw the students’ disciplinary hearings; and Wright. District spokesman Dan Hollar declined comment on the lawsuit Tuesday. A criminal investigation is ongoing. “(The Boise Police Department) has reviewed the evidence currently available and will continue to evaluate additional evidence as it is received from the social media platforms,” spokeswoman Haley Kramer said in an email Tuesday. “It is anticipated that it will take time to receive and evaluate this additional evidence and interview additional witnesses based on that new information.” More reading : Click here for coverage from the Idaho Statesman, which first reported on the lawsuit.

The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. (Photo by Barb Barrett/Stateline) States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines continue to mount, costing Americans nearly $389 million last year alone. Four states — Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont — enacted statewide bans this year, while dozens of communities have moved to prohibit the machines or impose new restrictions on their use. A new law in Hawaii, which went into effect in October, bans consumers from depositing cash into kiosks to buy cryptocurrency. The crackdown comes as scammers increasingly direct victims to cryptocurrency kiosks, often located in gas stations, convenience stores and grocery stores, to deposit cash that is converted into digital currency and transferred to accounts controlled by criminals. The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. Complaints increased 23% from the previous year, while financial losses jumped 58%, according to the agency’s cybercrime report, which was released in April. Older Americans have been particularly hard hit. More than half of the complaints involved people older than 50, who reported more than $302 million in losses last year. The mounting losses have prompted policymakers across the country to pursue tighter restrictions and outright bans on cryptocurrency kiosks — efforts that consumer advocates say are urgently needed to prevent further financial harm. “Every day that these laws aren’t passed are days where victims are having money stolen from them, and that money, because it’s through cryptocurrency and the nature of the kiosk, it’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back,” said Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director, in an interview with Stateline. Indiana became the first state to ban cryptocurrency kiosks in March, followed by Tennessee and Vermont in July and Minnesota in August. The measures mark a shift from earlier efforts to regulate the machines through transaction limits, fraud warnings and licensing requirements. items.body: After months of waiting, last week the Idaho State Tax Commission finally released information about which parents are receiving the $50 million in voucher money. Surprise, surprise, the Tax Commission report says most of the money is going to families that earn more than double the income of the average Idahoan and students who have never attended public schools. The average family that received voucher money this year earned $178,000, more than double the $84,234 of the average Idaho family. This makes the voucher program a government handout for families who can already afford to send their kids to private schools. Moreover, 75 percent of the families who took the money have never had their kids enrolled in a public school, even though advocates for the program promised that it would help students leave so-called “failing public schools” to attend private ones. And of the 25 percent of families whose kids did attend a public school, only 4.6 percent were enrolled for an entire school year a year ago. Critics of the voucher program warned that it would mainly benefit families living in urban areas rather than in rural communities. As expected, two thirds of the voucher money went to families living in just three counties – Ada, Canyon, and Kootenai. Furthermore, nearly 25 percent of the money went to only five private schools, most of them religious schools: Bishop Kelly High School in Boise, Cole Valley Christian in Meridian, Nampa Christian School, The Ambrose School in Meridian and Logos Classical Christian School in Moscow which is led by Christian Nationalist Doug Wilson. Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, a retired teacher, was one of the leading opponents of the voucher program and on Friday reacted to the Tax Commission report: “It’s hard enough for working parents to make ends meet without being asked to subsidize private school tuition for families who are better off than they are.” Ward-Engelking said someone should “explain to a rural parent why their child’s school can’t afford another teacher, but the state can afford to help a well-off family pay private school tuition. That’s a pretty lousy deal for rural Idaho.” Nothing in this report should be a surprise to Governor Brad Little or the legislators who voted to create the voucher program. They were warned that voucher programs across the country benefit the rich, and families that never sent their kids to public schools, and urban families over rural families. Still, Republican legislators, most of them rural, voted for vouchers and Governor Little signed it into law, even though 32,000 Idahoans contacted his office and asked him to veto the bill. Vouchers, which are unpopular among most citizens, was one of the major issues in the country during the recent mid-term election. The issue contributed to the election of Democratic governors and legislators in many Republican states which adopted vouchers. In Texas, longtime Republican Governor Greg Abbott, the leading advocate for school vouchers in the Lone Star State, lost to a Democrat who made her reputation by opposing vouchers while serving in the Legislature. In Arizona, voters not only re-elected Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs by a comfortable margin but elected a Democratic majority in both houses of the Arizona Legislature for the first time since 1966. In Iowa and Ohio, where Republican governors and legislators have expanded voucher programs, voters elected a Democratic governor for the first time in years. Unfortunately, in Idaho voters did not have a chance to weigh in on the voucher issue with accurate information about who it benefits. As a result, only one of the 62 Republican legislators who voted for the voucher bill lost their seat in the recent election. You cannot blame voters – they didn’t have the information on which to base their votes. items.body: A Boise State University Ph.D. student filed a tort claim alleging the university refused to assemble the mandatory dissertation committee required to finish his degree. Jeffrey Morgan is seeking damages of at least $1.5 million, according to the Oct. 15 claim. The university declined to comment on the claim, through Stephany Galbreaith, d irector of media relations. Morgan finished all coursework for his Ph.D. in Boise State’s Public Policy and Administration Program with a 4.0 GPA, according to the claim. As he moved toward his final step — completing his dissertation — the university rejected his proposal and entered an F grade. Morgan appealed the grade this spring. On April 29, the university acknowledged programmatic failures led to the failing grade and wiped it from his transcript, according to the claim. Interim program director Jaclyn Kettler wrote in an April 22 letter to the university’s registrar that “some program-level issues contributed to his challenges” with the course. The university hadn’t offered a key course on developing dissertation proposals when Morgan needed it because of a shortage of faculty available to teach it, Kettler wrote. “For reasons completely outside of his control, he was in a disadvantaged position in terms of his proposal development — making it harder to be successful in the course,” Kettler wrote. Program leadership and faculty turnover also contributed to the issue, Kettler said. Morgan needed to find a new dissertation chair and committee, which was “quite challenging” due to the number of faculty retiring or leaving the university. On April 30, the registrar approved removing the course from Morgan’s transcript, according to an email attached to the tort claim. The university is in the midst of merging the College of Education and School of Public Service. The merger, which will happen over the course of two years, won’t impact students, Andrew Finstuen, the interim dean, said this spring. The university did not respond to questions about the Public Policy and Administration PhD program. Morgan’s claim states that the university offered a transfer option that isn’t viable because Morgan would lose all the credits he already completed in the doctoral program. “Rather than correcting the structural issue by appointing a functional committee, the university administration left Claimant in a permanent academic blockade, offering only a disingenuous “transfer” that nullified years of labor and passing of comprehensive exams,” the claim reads. Morgan estimates lost wages of $1.5 million ($60,000 per year for 25 years as a non-tenure-track faculty member). He also estimates $15,000 in student loan-related losses.

The audits, required by a 2022 state law , are meant to verify the accuracy of election results reported by counties, which run elections locally. There, officials recounted all ballots as a cautionary measure after they found more than 2,300 ballots from early voting had not been reported on Election Day. items.body: The Idaho Tax Commission has released its first in-depth report on year one of the state’s new parental choice tax credit, and the overwhelming evidence shows it has been a monumental success. The analysis, released Friday, documents 12,216 final student awards, $49.3 million allocated for educational assistance, and awarded parent applications in every legislative district in Idaho. In addition, there are now 137 families on the tax credit waitlist. Those are substantial results for a program that has spent much of its early existence under political attack – from both legislators who have sought to defund it and activists who tried to knock it down in court. Both efforts proved unsuccessful. In full, the analysis gives Idaho a strong foundation on which to build—and good reason to focus on helping more families participate. The data shows that, of 6,875 awarded parents, 3,075 (or 44.7%) qualified under the program’s income priority, meaning their income on their 2024 return was at or below 300% of the federal poverty level. That number will vary based on household size. It includes families below the poverty line and families earning up to three times that threshold. Despite the claims that money would only be allocated to those living in Boise, Ada and Canyon counties account for just over half of awarded parents. More than 3,300 awarded parents—48% of the statewide total—are outside those two counties. They account for $22.64 million in educational assistance. In fact, on a per-capita basis, Idaho, Latah and Kootenai counties showed the largest participation rates. Eastern and southeastern Idaho provide another useful perspective, particularly given that most of the opposition to education choice came from those areas. Across the eight counties in that region, 647 parents were awarded help worth $4.27 million. Bannock and Bonneville counties alone account for 461 awarded parents and nearly $3 million. The report also shows families using different educational arrangements. Approximately one in five awarded students is homeschooling or planning to homeschool. The school table lists homeschool awards averaging approximately $2,776, accounting for about 19% of student awards but only 13% of award dollars. Separately, 3,092 awarded students—25.3%—had previously attended public school. Families are also reporting expenses beyond tuition. Although tuition accounts for 93.5% of expenses claimed to date, the remaining categories total approximately $2.5 million, including more than $1 million for curricula, approximately $600,000 for tutoring, $544,000 for transportation, and $246,000 for textbooks. These are practical expenses that every family may experience. There is no evidence of any Idaho parents submitting reimbursement requests for large screen TV’s or vacations. This is important to note given the prediction of opponents who claimed that funds would be abused. Now that we know the Idaho Parental Tax Credit to be such a roaring success, what should Idaho do with these findings? First, we should help approved families receive the assistance already allocated to them. The report identifies 430 parents who filed returns without claiming approved credits totaling $2.1 million. Some filed before receiving approval and may need to amend their returns. Second, we should examine the 1,232 applications that were started but not completed or submitted. Third, lawmakers should consider additional capacity. The current allocation averages approximately $4,038 per final student award. Holding that average and the current administrative share constant, a $75 million annual budget could help a total of approximately 18,300 students, about 6,100 more than current capacity. A $100 million budget could support some 24,400 students. Skeptics of Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit have done everything possible to stop, obstruct and delay the program. The tax credit was one of the most discussed bills of 2025, and critics said it marked a major shift in education policy by making state funding available for private school tuition and expenses outside of the state’s K-12 public school system. items.body: Idaho’s private education tax credit is primarily subsidizing tuition for wealthy families whose children were already enrolled in a private school, according to a report released Friday. The Idaho State Tax Commission, for the first time, released a wide range of data that sheds light on the beneficiaries of the $50 million, taxpayer-funded Parental Choice Tax Credit program. GOP members of the Legislature and Republican Gov. Brad Little created the state’s first private school choice program last year through House Bill 93. Here are some of the highlights from the report: 12,216 students received a tax credit or advance payment. 80.7% attend a private school and 19.3% are home schooling. 74.7% have never attended a public school. $178,000 is the average adjusted gross income for recipient households. 1.7 is the average number of students per household that received a credit. 55.5% of households earn more and 44.5% earn less than 300% of the federal poverty level, a benchmark determining who had the first dibs on the credits. 93.5% of tax credits covered tuition expenses. In other words, the typical credit covered private school tuition for a family of four that earns $178,000 and whose children never attended a public school. Idaho’s median household income is $84,234, according to U.S. Census data. Friday’s report undermines a key selling point of the bitterly debated private school choice program: that it would help students who couldn’t otherwise afford private education options. “Idahoans were sold a lie about this voucher scheme,” House Minority Leader Ilana Rubel, D-Boise, said in a news release Friday. “We were told this program would help low-income children leave public schools for supposedly better-performing private schools. Instead, more than half of the families awarded tax credits are above the income threshold Republicans promised to prioritize, and nearly three-quarters of students have never attended an Idaho public school.” The refundable tax credit offers Idaho students, regardless of their family’s income, up to $5,000 — or $7,500 if they have special needs — to reimburse their non-public education costs, including tuition, curriculum and tutoring, among other things. Idaho Education News and others had sought data on the program’s rollout for months, but the Tax Commission denied records requests, promising a report by January. The agency ultimately published the report earlier than expected but 10 days after the Nov. 3 election, when all 105 state lawmakers and the governor were up for re-election. “Voters deserved this information before casting their ballots,” Rubel said. “We should repeal this program or, at the very least, end subsidies for higher-income families.” However, the report includes more data than HB 93 required. A provision in the bill told the Tax Commission to compile a report on the program’s first year with several data points. But it didn’t call for the percentage of students who previously attended a public school. In a statement Friday, Little said his administration “went above and beyond to provide as much information and data as possible while protecting taxpayers’ personal information.” “This report gives policymakers and the public a clearer picture of the program and provides the best available data to evaluate its effectiveness, identify opportunities for improvement, and ensure it continues to serve Idahoans well,” Little said in a news release. Emily Callihan, Little’s communications director, declined EdNews’ request to interview the governor Friday. EdNews also reached out to tax commissioner Janet Moyle along with Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog and House Majority Leader Jason Monks. The Republican lawmakers from Meridian co-sponsored HB 93 along with former Rep. Wendy Horman, a Republican from Idaho Falls, who now works for the Trump administration.
