items.body: Campaign signs greet attendees at the election night watch party for independent U.S. Senate Candidate Todd Achilles on Nov. 3, 2026, in Garden City, Idaho. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s Todd Achilles was one of a handful of major independent U.S. Senate candidates in red states to generate national attention ahead of the 2026 general election. Although he and the other high-profile independents lost their races, Achilles argues there’s still a future for independents to be a competitive alternative in a two-party system, and a viable way to win in such a Republican state. U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, talks to an Idaho News 6 reporter at the Idaho GOP election night watch party at the Grove in Boise, Idaho, on Nov. 8, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Achilles, a former Democratic state legislator, ended with 33.57% of the vote, compared to incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch’s 56.6% in the four-way race with no Democrat on the ballot. The other independent candidate, Natalie Fleming, received around 7% of the vote. In an election year where many Republicans struggled in nationwide federal races, Idaho voters stood by their GOP incumbents. “Idaho is different because, it’s just the advantage for Republicans among voter behavior is so outsized compared to even states in the South,” said Robert Jones, a partner and political strategist at Boise-based GS Strategy Group. Nearly 62% of Idaho voters are registered with the Republican Party, and 12% are registered Democrats, according to the Idaho secretary of state’s office . More than 24% aren’t affiliated with either party. Voters who deeply align with a major political party tend to stick with that party, even when they aren’t necessarily satisfied with their performance, said Idaho State University political scientist Edward Greer. Greer researches American politics, political psychology, and political behavior. “If a political party is not meeting those needs, then there’s not typically going to be a lot of crossover to the other side,” Greer said. “Usually, people will just kind of sit out.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Was this race different from past Idaho U.S. Senate elections? The win, although still comfortable, was Risch’s closest general election race since he first won his U.S. Senate seat in 2008. In 2008, Risch won with 57.7% of the vote against Democratic challenger and former congressman Larry LaRocco, who had 34.1% of the vote, with three other candidates on the ballot. Achilles, speaking to the Idaho Capital Sun the day after the election, said his campaign “built a great foundation” for the independent movement in Idaho. Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Todd Achilles speaks with attendees at an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, at Iconic Bistro and Bar in Garden City. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “We went from zero to 33% in 18 months,” he said. “… We got a lot of people excited. We had hundreds of meetings and town halls and events across the state. Everything I’m seeing in my inbox this morning is, ‘Let’s keep going.’ ‘We like what this independent movement is about.’” Achilles said he hasn’t decided if he would run again, but that he plans to continue to be involved in politics. His campaign garnered a similar share of votes as Democrats in other statewide races. Risch’s last challenger, Democrat Paulette Jordan, finished with a similar vote share, with 33.2% in the 2020 election. Achilles this year narrowly outperformed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens, who won 32.25% of the vote in her five-way contest against incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little. A federal judge in Idaho dismissed a lawsuit in December against an Idaho law that bans vaccine and other medical mandates, including in private businesses. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) A Boise daycare that is challenging an Idaho law that bans vaccine and other medical mandates in businesses, schools and government has appealed a lower court decision throwing out its case. In September, a federal judge in Idaho dismissed a lawsuit that argued the Idaho Medical Freedom Act was unconstitutionally vague, among other claims. But late last month, a Boise daycare and parents who sought to block the law from applying to daycares appealed the ruling to a federal appeals court. The case, now before the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, is awaiting arguments from both sides. The state law, passed in 2025 , bans businesses, governments and schools from mandating vaccines or “medical interventions,” which are defined as: “a medical procedure, treatment, device, drug injection, medication, or medical action taken to diagnose, prevent, or cure a disease or alter the health or biological function of a person.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE In a ruling granting Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s request to dismiss the lawsuit , Chief U.S. District Judge for the District of Idaho Amanda K. Brailsford wrote she agreed with Labrador’s interpretation of the law’s definition of “medical interventions,” writing that they refer to health actions that are “medical in nature.” “The (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) plainly and unambiguously sets out a standard of prohibited conduct that gives a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited,” Brailsford wrote. An attorney for the suing parties — Le Soleil Child Care LLC, and three parents whose kids attend the daycare or hope to — declined to comment. Labrador’s office couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. Republican Idaho Gov. Brad Little vetoed an earlier version of the law over concerns that it could prevent schools from sending home sick kids. But in April, his spokesperson said the revised bill that the governor signed into law “does not jeopardize the ability of public schools or daycares to send home children sick with contagious conditions.” Labrador, also a Republican, urged lawmakers to override the governor’s veto. items.body: Idaho public school enrollment dropped by 8,983 students this fall, or 2.9% over the summer, according to data provided by the Idaho Department of Education. There are 304,871 students enrolled in schools across Idaho, down from 313,854 at the end of last school year. This is the largest enrollment drop in at least 10 years, and the drop continues a yearslong trend. A number of factors can impact school enrollment, from birth rates to home prices to school choice. The biggest winners — charter schools, which gained nearly a thousand students, propelled by the fall opening of seven. The biggest losers — traditional districts, including Idaho’s largest West Ada. The Boise School district, Idaho’s second largest, continued its years-long losing trend with a drop of more than 1,000. All but 15 of 117 districts lost students. Virtual schools, either charters or those governed by districts, also showed big losses. The migration away from virtual schools and possibly to homeschooling or private schools coincides with the first year of the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit, which 12,561 students applied for. The funds, up to $5,000 per student or $7,500 for a student with special needs, can be used to cover homeschooling costs and private school tuition. But very little is known about who received the tax credit, after requests for demographic data were denied. Enrollment numbers change throughout the year as students move and schools correct data inputs. Districts report enrollment to the state monthly. EdNews compared 2026 spring counts to this fall for this story. Enrollment change varies by age and school type Idaho’s enrollment decline is concentrated among elementary students, while enrollment continues to grow in middle and high schools, EdNews reported earlier this year. Idaho’s population continues to increase, with over 2 million residents statewide, but just 8% of growth is attributed to school-aged children, according to Idaho Department of Labor Economist Lisa Grigg. Charter schools showed a net gain of about 515 students. New charter schools accounted for 2,124 students, ranging from 658 at Brabion Academy to 14 at Trailhead Virtual Academy. The largest charter enrollment loss was at Idaho Home Learning Academy, with 742 students. IHLA came under fire last legislative session after a report found payments to families of up to $1,800 were spent inappropriately. Payments have more guardrails on how they’re spent this year. At the same time, families could apply for a larger tax credit to homeschool. Virtual public schools received a $3 million funding cut last session. Enrollment in both charter and district-run online schools dropped last year. Quick facts: 39 of 82 charter schools gained or maintained enrollment. 43 charter schools lost enrollment. 15 of 117 traditional public school districts gained or maintained enrollment. 102 traditional districts lost enrollment. The largest enrollment gain in a traditional district was 30 students (8%) in tiny Plummer-Worley. Only small districts gained enrollment, except for Lakeland, which added two students to its 4,650 total. items.body: Two music teachers are orchestrating the resistance to artificial intelligence in Idaho. Boise couple Jack and Cathryn Gardner have organized the state’s first AI protest. They’ve been meeting with federal and state lawmakers to push for regulations on the technology, and they’re seeing firsthand how AI influences young students. Cathryn teaches music to elementary students in the Boise School District and Jack, who formerly taught music in the Nampa School District, is a freelance bassist teaching private lessons to high school and college students. “I see it affecting how my students are thinking critically and thinking cognitively,” Cathryn told Idaho Education News in an interview last month. “But I’m seeing, too, that it’s affecting their ability to process and to work independently and to think creatively.” Jack and Cathryn co-lead the Boise chapter of PauseAI US . The nationwide advocacy group’s goal is to tighten government regulation on AI development to prevent “adversarial superintelligence,” rogue AI agents that disobey humans. The couple holds monthly meetups and tables weekly at community events. Their first protest, held Oct. 24 in front of the Idaho Statehouse, included speeches from volunteers and signs and flyers advocating for humanism, reported The Arbiter, Boise State University’s campus newspaper. Meanwhile, Jack and Cathryn have been meeting with lawmakers, including U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson and Sen. Jim Risch, to advocate for regulations on AI. They’ve been featured in The New York Times . PauseAI US leaders consider the couple their “best organizers,” and praise their ability to break down complex AI concerns for people without technical knowledge. “ I think they’re a great example of like, yeah, any person can go meet with the senator, raise the alarm, and propose some good ideas, and together we can solve the problem,” said Alvaro Cuba, associate director at PauseAI. Jack Gardner, left, with U.S. Senator Jim Risch. (Jack Gardner photo) Music teachers grow concerned with AI Making music is one of the few remaining activities that only humans can do, Jack said, a nd a s artificial intelligence proliferates education and the workforce, the Gardners are putting humanity at the center of their lessons. “ AI noise isn’t really music,” Jack said. “…Studying an instrument teaches delayed gratification, which is the polar opposite of what AI promises and doesn’t deliver. Being in an ensemble teaches you human interaction skills that they’re not getting in their online lives.” When it comes to AI’s broader impact on society, Jack had been focused on the technology stealing musicians’ work without credit or compensation. Then, last year, he learned about the hypothesis that AI’s progress could lead to the extinction of humanity. This summer, rogue AI agents made real-life headlines after OpenAI’s agents breached containment and hacked Hugging Face , an open-source AI development platform. Jack knew he had to do something about it. He and Cathryn searched for anti-AI organizations and joined Pause AI in August of 2025. They founded PauseAI Boise shortly after. items.body: School trustees want Idaho to bring its K-12 funding model into the 21 st century. No, really, they do. Convening in Boise last week, the state’s school trustees overwhelmingly passed three different resolutions calling for changes to a much-maligned and aging school funding formula, which was last modified in 1994. The trustees aren’t alone. State superintendent Debbie Critchfield, easily re-elected to a second term last week, has made a funding formula rewrite her top priority. But the big question mark is still Gov. Brad Little, also easily re-elected last week. In his first two terms, Little has supported Idaho’s current school funding approach, while keeping his options open. Any funding formula rewrite must go through Little. Predictably enough, Little isn’t committing himself. For those just checking in — or those who need a refresher — here’s a summary of the debate, and what’s at stake. Attendance vs. enrollment The formula has long been based on student attendance. And Little has been on board with this status quo approach. Supporters of an attendance-based model want schools to have an incentive to get (and keep) kids in classroom seats. Supporters of a rewrite, such as Critchfield, point out that those kids in the seats are fundamentally different. It costs more to teach a special education student, an English language learner, or a gifted and talented student. They also point out that students are more mobile than they were in 1994 — more likely to split up their schedule, instead of spending their entire day in one building. Hence the argument for an enrollment-based model that reflects individual student needs and student schedules. The funding formula drives the largest distribution of dollars in the state budget — the $2.8 billion in tax revenues that go out to K-12 schools. The high stakes help explain why elected officials and education lobbyists have haggled over a rewrite for a decade. items.body: Next year marks the second consecutive year of double digit premium rate increases across Your Health Idaho plans. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images) For about the next month, Idahoans can enroll in health insurance plans on the state’s exchange. As health insurance premiums continue to grow, Idaho’s exchange, Your Health Idaho, is the only place that Idahoans can go to get private health insurance discounted by the federal government. For some Idahoans, that discount — in the form of a tax credit — might shield them from the average of 12% premium rises for plans on the exchange, said Your Health Idaho Executive Director Pat Kelly. That’s because the tax credit is linked to the cost of one slate of plans, the silver, he said. “We’re actually seeing net premiums — which is the amount consumers pay after the tax credit is applied — we’re seeing those net premiums either flat or declining in 2027,” Kelly said in an interview. He offered a few examples of how that could work. A single person in Ada County earning $36,000 a year might pay $8 less in premiums. If that person lived in the Magic Valley, they might pay $30 less in premiums, he said. “Health insurance, for those that receive a tax credit, is an incredible affordability story this year,” Kelly said. “They’re actually seeing plans that are either the same net premium cost from ‘26 to ‘27, or actually a decrease, which is just unheard of these days.” But he stressed that the tax credit’s application depends on your family’s specifics: Where you live, how big your household is, and how much you make. So he encouraged Idahoans to use Your Health Idaho’s online tool to estimate how much of a tax credit they’d receive. Congress last year didn’t renew bigger discounts on federal and state exchanges, but there are still smaller discounts baked into the federal Affordable Care Act, which led to the exchanges’ creation. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits last year led about 25,000 Idahoans to cancel plans on the state exchange, Your Health Idaho estimated. Next year marks the second consecutive year of double digit premium rate increases across Your Health Idaho plans. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE When is open enrollment? And how do I sign up and shop around? Open enrollment for Your Health Idaho lasts until Dec. 15. The cutoff that day is 11:59 p.m. Mountain time. Coverage for new plans starts Jan. 1. On the exchange, Idahoans can pick from 143 medical plans and 32 dental plans from 12 insurance companies. At the state exchange’s website , you can shop for plans, see how much in a tax credit you could qualify for, use an affordability tool and find an agent or broker who can help you free of cost. Find pop-up enrollment centers hosted by Your Health Idaho online . Your Health Idaho officials say you shouldn’t wait until the last minute to enroll. For the most part, open enrollment is the last time that Idahoans can enroll in Your Health Idaho before next fall, unless they have a qualifying life event . “Start early, bring your questions, and let a local expert help you find coverage that fits your life and your budget,” Marcia Benton, a broker in Meridian, said in a written statement. (Photo by Christophe Paul/U.S. Department of Agriculture) Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest resting place for America’s heroes, is sacred ground for our veterans. As we commemorate Veterans Day this year, we should turn our thoughts and pay our respects to the many Idahoans who have been laid to rest in that hallowed ground. They include two Congressional Medal of Honor winners. Col. Reginald Rodney Myers , who was born in Boise, earned the Medal of Honor for valor in the vicious Battle of Chosin Reservoir in Korea in November of 1950. First Lt. Vernon J. Baker, who was born in Wyoming, but lived his last 15 years in Idaho, received the Medal of HOnor for conspicuous valor near Viareggio, Italy, in April of 1945. His award came 52 years late because of his black skin. A number of Idahoans from Vietnam and subsequent wars are interred in the peaceful environs of Arlington. In July of 2012, the remains of Chief Master Sgt. Larry Thornton of Idaho Falls were buried at Arlington , 45 years after his AC-47D took off from Vietnam on Christmas Eve of 1965 and disappeared over Laos. I’ve been to Arlington many times since my Vietnam service. Every time I saw the grave marker of a Vietnam comrade, I was flooded with profound grief and anger for the 58,220 American lives taken by that ill-fated war, including 251 with Idaho connections. Those emotions were always somewhat assuaged by the quiet, dignified atmosphere of the cemetery. That calming atmosphere is currently facing a serious threat from another Donald Trump vanity project. Trump’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch will sit smack dab in front of Arlington Cemetery, destroying its peace and tranquility, as well as the symmetry and symbolism of its location. The National Park Service dared to report that the arch “would break alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House that was Robert E. Lee’s home.” It continued: “The bridge alignment and associated ceremonial landscape were intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River.” It has also been noted that the arch requires an act of Congress. It does not have congressional approval, but that has never stopped Trump from bullying ahead. Trump is not the first president to propose construction that would have severely interfered with that alignment, as well as the pastoral atmosphere of the cemetery. President Franklin D. Why build an arch in the first place? The Romans were among the first of the ancients to construct triumphal arches. They made an art of building arches to recognize victorious generals returning from battle. It is not clear why Trump would be entitled to an arch on that basis because his Iran War has been an unmitigated disaster for our country. The Iranians have kept what remains of their nuclear material. The war has caused skyrocketing prices for gas, diesel, fertilizer, and most consumer goods that need to be transported. Passing the moratorium means Boise will not accept or process any applications for large data centers that fall within the moratorium’s parameters. “It’s a six-month moratorium that will put the brakes on hyperscale data centers in Boise, so it gives us the time to better determine and understand the impacts that these will have,” said Boise Mayor Lauren McLean, who proposed the moratorium Friday. McLean said the city does not currently have any large data center applications pending. “I’m doing this now before we have an application so that we can be sure that we get it right,” McLean said. Boise city officials will use the moratorium to review code and policies, study the impact on water, energy use, wastewater, noise and public safety, and gather public feedback. Chief of Staff Hannah Brass Greer said Boise’s existing code does not address data centers. “One of the things we would be doing is looking at our code and where it would fit and what restrictions or guidelines we want to put in place,” Brass Greer said. items.body: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images) Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has survived an impeachment effort, at least for now, after the U.S. House on Tuesday blocked a vote over charges that the Cabinet official oversaw extrajudicial killings and an illegal war against Iran. The House voted 211-204 , largely along party lines, to refer articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a committee — effectively killing the impeachment effort until the end of the current Congress in January. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans missed the vote. The vote came hours after Hegseth defended himself in a fiery news conference at the Pentagon, where he denounced the impeachment effort as an attack on American service members. He called the bid to remove him a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term. “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said. Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the Defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges. Impeachment would have represented an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon. On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. Hegseth’s opponents could try again to impeach him during the new Congress, which begins in January. Democrats will hold a large majority in the House at that time. Earlier in the day, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who will likely become majority leader when his party takes over the chamber, said Hegseth should stand trial in the Senate if impeached. “Hegseth is already trying to hide behind our troops, falsely claiming that Congress disapproves of our courageous servicemembers even though we have fought to bring them home for months,” Schumer said. President Donald Trump has so far stood by Hegseth. He praised the Defense secretary in multiple public remarks over the past two weeks, saying he’s “done a fantastic job” in reducing the number of “woke” four-star generals, and for conducting the “war with Venezuela,” which he said “was over in 48 minutes.” “Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday.

items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at Borah High School in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A week after the midterm election, Idaho election officials reported more than 300 ballots went uncounted on election night in an eastern Idaho county. The Office of the Idaho Secretary of State on Tuesday afternoon announced that 333 uncounted ballots had been identified during a post-election review in one precinct in Bannock County. State election officials said no outcomes changed once the ballots had been counted. The votes will be added to the state’s election results website Tuesday, officials added. Election recount planned in North Idaho county that didn’t report 2,300 ballots “Once again, this demonstrates the importance of the reconciliation process we use to verify election results following every election,” Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican who was reelected as the state’s top election official, said in a written statement. “While I am thankful that these ballots were identified, we will be working to determine why these ballots were not processed on election night and working with counties across the state to reinforce our election processes.” This is at least the second Idaho county to report it left some ballots unreported in election results after last week’s election. State election officials on Tuesday were overseeing a recount of ballots in North Idaho’s Latah County , after the county reported more than 2,300 ballots went unreported in election results. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE All of the uncounted ballots in Bannock County came from the same precinct, named Pocatello 2, state officials said. The county has 57 precincts. The closest race for any races that precinct was voting in, state officials say, is for county coroner, where Republican Torey Danner led independent candidate Wilson Simmons by 4,857 votes. The Bannock County Elections office, which features a ballot dropbox, is located on North Sixth Avenue in Pocatello, Idaho. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun) The precinct also voted in Legislative District 29, where Democrats swept all three seats . But in two of those races, Democrats had led by around 2,000 votes over Republicans, according to election results. The Idaho Office of Secretary of State soon corrected its announcement about the uncounted ballots. Bannock County Clerk Jason Dixon, the local election official, said in a statement that “this should not have happened.” “We take pride in Bannock County in the work that goes into running our elections,” Dixon said. “We are working closely with the Secretary of State’s office to ensure full transparency and to determine if additional steps can be taken to ensure this does not happen. I want Bannock County voters to know your votes will count.” The Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which certifies the state’s election results, is set to meet at 1 p.m. Friday to select counties and precincts that will undergo audits of election results, including hand counts and reviews of reported results. “We have numerous safeguards in place to verify the accuracy of Idaho’s elections,” McGrane said. “My main focus throughout all of this is to ensure that every single vote is counted and that Idahoans have confidence that their voice is heard.” The Bannock County Board of Commissioners is set to meet 9 a.m. Thursday to recanvass the election results, including the added ballots. items.body: After InvestigateWest and Invisible Institute filed a lawsuit seeking the records, Ada County District Judge Patrick J. Miller ordered Idaho State Police and Idaho Department of Correction to release information about officers’ employment history, including the dates of their employment and the reason for their separation. (InvestigateWest illustration) This article originally published in InvestigateWest on Nov. 10. Idaho State Police and the Idaho Department of Correction improperly withheld police employment records and other information from two news organizations, according to a state court ruling ordering the information be released. InvestigateWest and the Invisible Institute sued the state agencies on June 16 for allegedly concealing information about officers’ employment histories that were previously disclosed to the news outlets. InvestigateWest used officer employment records to expose alleged sexual misconduct by dozens of Idaho prison guards in an October 2025 series , and to show how many were allowed to resign without facing other disciplinary action or criminal prosecution. The reporting prompted Idaho lawmakers to remove a loophole in a sexual abuse law that made it more difficult for prosecutors to charge prison staff, and to order an independent review of how the women’s prison system handles reports of sexual abuse. After those stories were published, reporters from InvestigateWest and the Invisible Institute sought updated officer employment records, but the Department of Correction and state police denied those requests, stating that they would no longer disclose whether an officer retired, resigned or was fired. A records clerk also told the Invisible Institute that Idaho State Police leadership decided to “disable” a tool that allowed them to search an internal employment database. In a Nov. 5 ruling, Ada County District Judge Patrick J. Miller ordered the state agencies to release information about officers’ employment history, including the dates of their employment and the reason for their separation. That includes information about two former prison guards accused of sexually assaulting an inmate, who described the assaults and the mental toll it took on her to an InvestigateWest reporter. “This ruling is a win for government transparency — and accountability — in Idaho,” said Jacob Fries, InvestigateWest’s executive director. “These public records had been essential to our reporter’s work, which led directly to a new state law helping protect incarcerated people from abuses of power.” State law broadly defines “employment history” to include the entire course of a person’s employment, from when it started to the nature of how it ended, Judge Miller wrote, concluding that whether someone was terminated, retired or resigned is public information. The agencies argued that disclosing an officer was terminated, for example, would suggest potential disciplinary action against the individual, and that legislators specifically exempted disciplinary details from disclosure. Idaho State Police also claimed the requested employment history information was contained in confidential decertification files that it said are exempt. Judge Miller said disclosing the reason for separation doesn’t amount to revealing the underlying details behind an employee’s departure. And just because an officer’s employment history and dates of service are in the same file as confidential details doesn’t mean they “lose their character” as disclosable records, the judge wrote. The Idaho Public Records Act “does not categorically shield every piece of information contained within an otherwise exempt file. items.body: Sierra Bohamera is all about algorithms. Both in her math classroom at Capital High School, and on TikTok, where she shares her life and lessons to her 500,000 followers. Growing up in Bend, Ore., Bohamera always loved school. Teachers were the people she looked up to in life. “I thought they were the coolest people ever,” Bohamera said. “They made me feel very welcome in class and inspired to try.” As a high schooler, Bohamera interned at a local elementary school and was hooked. She moved to Idaho to attend Boise State University. She student taught in kindergarten and loved it. But a second student teaching experience in her minor subject area, math, proved to be transformative. Bohamera struggled in math until the fifth grade, when she had a teacher who let her make mistakes then helped her work through the issue to get the right answer. At the time, Bohamera was shy and the teacher would encourage her to “share your thinking with the class.” That experience taught Bohamera she can do hard things and it’s a moment she still thinks about 20 years later. Still, Bohamera didn’t see herself as solely a math teacher, so she was shocked to find she enjoyed working with teenagers. She loved the challenge of earning older students’ trust, especially when they come in a bit apprehensive. “Math can be intimidating for kids,” Bohamera said. “A lot of times if they don’t get it right away they feel like they’re dumb.” Now in her eighth year at Capital High, “Miss Bo,” as she’s known, focuses on making class fun. Instead of a worksheet with practice problems, students compete in groups to solve problems quickly. “All of a sudden they’ve done 20 problems,” Bohamera said. “They want to get the right answer so they can beat the other team.” She focuses on positive reinforcement, building on individual students’ strengths to tackle problems they may struggle with. The goal is to teach students not just math, but that they can do hard things, Bohamera said. The students love Bohamera, said Principal Derek Gardner, in part because she connects with them. “It’s not just a math class where you put your head down and are working by yourself sort of the more traditional way,” Gardner said. “It’s almost the exact opposite of that.” It’s rarely quiet when Gardner walks by Bohamera’s room. “It’s a very productive noise,” he said. Click to view slideshow. Part of that connection comes from Bohamera’s goal of being a role model both in and out of the classroom, he said. Since 2021, Bohamera has posted on TikTok about her life as a teacher. She posts teacher outfits, lesson ideas, and her adventures around Boise as “ThatTrendyTeacher.” She garnered more than 500,000 followers on TikTok and another few hundred thousand on Instagram. “I initially downloaded it because I wanted to connect more with students,” Bohamera said. Her hope now is to show her followers and students what a well rounded lifestyle is with a good work life balance. “I always kind of post with the lense of my student is watching and my school is watching,” Bohamera said. “When you grow up, and if you want to do similar things, you can see a positive adult role model in your life.” Especially at a time when there can be negativity online about the profession and public schools, Bohamera hopes to show people that there are teachers who love their job and have fun doing it. The goal for Bohamera is to make her class about more than math; it’s about life. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images) U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone Tuesday as he faces potential impeachment by the U.S. House of Representatives this week, casting the effort as an attack on American service members. Hegseth during a rare news conference at the Pentagon called the impeachment effort a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term. “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said. The House, led by Republicans during the lame-duck session following the Nov. 3 election, is set to vote on impeaching Hegseth as soon as Wednesday, with a procedural vote expected later Tuesday. Massie impeachment articles Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges. Impeachment would represent an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Democrats, as well as some Republicans, are expected to support the effort, raising the possibility the articles will pass and trigger a trial in the Senate, though the outcome is unclear there. Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon. On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. items.body: Boise State University is shifting millions of dollars into its athletics programs to protect a “truly global” brand, President David Hahn says. The funding shift could also allow Boise State to ride through a turbulent time in college sports — where schools can now spend up to $21.6 million in “revenue sharing” payments to student athletes. “The landscape has changed so rapidly,” Hahn said in the latest edition of The EdNews Show . “It’s an arms race.” The State Board of Education is allowing Boise State to use reserves to cover up to $18 million in athletics deficits. Hahn hopes the short-term plan will buy Boise State some “stability,” as Congress considers an overhaul of college athletics. Meanwhile, he’s hoping to preserve Boise State’s athletics brand — which introduces Boise State to prospective applicants and donors. “Brands take decades and years to build, and they can be lost very quickly,” he said. “That brand has value far beyond the number of tickets we sell on a Saturday afternoon.” Hahn discussed several other topics in the EdNews interview. Here are a couple of quick highlights: Enrollment . Boise State’s fall student numbers are up, slightly. But with Idaho’s college-aged population likely to grow in future years — and with other states bracing for a population decrease — Boise State will face increased competition to recruit and retain in-state students. Boise State’s affordability and campus environment — and its athletics brand — are all potential selling points. “(We need to) be all we can be,” Hahn said. The political climate . Hahn, hired on July 1, said he is encouraged by his early conversations with legislators. The relationship between Boise State and the Legislature has been contentious for several years — resulting in budget cuts driven by skepticism about the university’s social justice agenda. But Hahn said the university is poised to capitalize on growth in Idaho, and especially in the Treasure Valley. “It’s our moment … and my job is to build the relationships, find that common ground. And it’s been going well.” This edition of the EdNews Show — and all previous episodes — are available on YouTube , Spotify or Apple Podcasts .

items.body: (UPDATED, 4:46 p.m., with more national context on Idaho’s funding decrease.) Idaho’s share of federal healthcare grants will decrease next year. The reasons for the reduction are unclear — and it’s too early to know how the cut will affect Idaho programs. In the second year of the feds’ five-year, $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program , Idaho will receive close to $182.7 million. Idaho’s first-year grant totaled $185.9 million. In a news release Monday, Gov. Brad Little’s office announced the Year Two grants — which could have far-reaching implications for K-12 and higher education programs. But the news release made no mention of the reduction. Little’s office has received no explanation of the reduction, spokeswoman Emily Callihan told EdNews in an email Monday afternoon. The state Department of Health and Welfare had no answers either, spokesman AJ McWhorter said Monday afternoon. The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services did not immediately respond to questions from EdNews. Idaho’s funding decrease comes to slightly more than $3.25 million — ranking as one of the steepest in the nation. Only nine states lost more healthcare grant dollars from Year One to Year Two. For months, state officials have said Idaho’s healthcare grant could increase — or decrease. The feds set up a competitive program, tying future payments to states’ track records. A state that met the feds’ deadlines and paperwork requirements could receive additional funding, at the expense of states that struggled. But Idaho met the feds’ Year One deadline. Idaho committed its $185.9 million in grants on Oct. 28, a couple of days ahead of schedule. More than $25 million of the first-year money will go to education-related programs: The biggest chunk, $12.5 million, will go into nearly a dozen “healthcare career advancement track” programs. Most of these projects are cooperative efforts involving two or more colleges and universities. All are designed to support rural students considering careers in healthcare fields. Another $8 million will go into fellowships and residencies, placing medical school graduates in rural Idaho. The University of Idaho will receive or share an additional $4.8 million in grants, Idaho State University will receive $2 million and Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and the Blind will receive nearly $900,000 for a mobile pediatric clinic. Decisions about spending the reduced grant will fall to a state agency in transition — and a legislative committee also facing a shakeup. Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron is stepping down later this year. An eight-member legislative committee is overseeing the grants; two committee members, Republican Reps. Dori Healey of Boise and Dustin Manwaring of Pocatello, were ousted in last week’s election . For Health and Welfare, the work is just getting started. “The (rural healthcare) program is in the process of reviewing the award and will be working with CMS to update the program’s workplan and budget,” McWhorter said Monday.

items.body: Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest resting place for America’s heroes, is sacred ground for our veterans. As we commemorate Veterans Day this year, we should turn our thoughts and pay our respects to the many Idahoans who have been laid to rest in that hallowed ground. They include two Congressional Medal of Honor winners. Colonel Reginald Rodney Myers , who was born in Boise, earned the MOH for valor in the vicious Battle of Chosin Reservoir in Korea in November of 1950. First Lieutenant Vernon J. Baker, who was born in Wyoming, but lived his last 15 years in Idaho, received the MOH for conspicuous valor near Viareggio, Italy, in April of 1945. His award came 52 years late because of his black skin. A number of Idahoans from Vietnam and subsequent wars are interred in the peaceful environs of Arlington. In July of 2012, the remains of Chief Master Sgt. Larry Thornton of Idaho Falls were buried at Arlington , 45 years after his AC-47D took off from Vietnam on Christmas Eve of 1965 and disappeared over Laos. I’ve been to Arlington many times since my Vietnam service. Every time I saw the grave marker of a Vietnam comrade, I was flooded with profound grief and anger for the 58,220 American lives taken by that ill-fated war, including 251 with Idaho connections. Those emotions were always somewhat assuaged by the quiet, dignified atmosphere of the Cemetery. That calming atmosphere is currently facing a serious threat from another Donald Trump vanity project. Trump’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch will sit smack dab in front of Arlington Cemetery, destroying its peace and tranquility, as well as the symmetry and symbolism of its location. The National Park Service dared to report that the arch “would break alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House that was Robert E. Lee’s home.” It continued: “The bridge alignment and associated ceremonial landscape were intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River.” It has also been noted that the arch requires an Act of Congress. It does not have Congressional approval, but that has never stopped Trump from bullying ahead. Trump is not the first president to propose construction that would have severely interfered with that alignment, as well as the pastoral atmosphere of the Cemetery. President Franklin D. Roosevelt proposed building the Pentagon in that location. He changed his mind after being convinced that it would obliterate the backdrop of tiered headstones and Arlington House. Why build an arch in the first place? The Romans were among the first of the ancients to construct triumphal arches. They made an art of building arches to recognize victorious generals returning from battle. It is not clear why Trump would be entitled to an arch on that basis because his Iran War has been an unmitigated disaster for our country. The Iranians have kept what remains of their nuclear material. The war has caused skyrocketing prices for gas, diesel, fertilizer, and most consumer goods that need to be transported. The explanation for the arch must lie elsewhere. Trump admitted last October that the monument was intended to honor “me” but later claimed it was to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. As he has continued to take flak for the project, Trump and his lackeys now contend it is required for the national defense. We already have a national defense project in the grand ballroom adjacent to the White House, but that does not seem to be sufficient in the president’s mind. In a shameful attempt to get around building restrictions, he now claims the arch will be laden with drones, snipers and machine guns so as to protect Washington from attack. If he had the slightest understanding of military tactics, he would understand that his arch would make an indefensible sitting-duck target. Not everyone is keen for Trump’s vanity arch. Federal authorities said on Monday Idaho will receive about $182.7 million in the second year of a grant designed to improve rural healthcare, marking a reduction from Idaho’s first-year award. The federal Rural Health Transformation grant was part of the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, in which Congress allocated $50 billion nationwide for the five-year program. The massive tax-and-spending bill also cut spending on Medicaid by about $1 trillion over 10 years — these reductions will start to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. Idaho was awarded nearly $186 million on Dec. 30, 2025, for the first year of the program. Idaho’s Republican Gov. Brad Little said in a press release. “That is especially important for families in rural Idaho, where distance and limited resources can create real barriers. This investment will help close those gaps, support local providers, and bring more care within reach for Idahoans across our state.” A spokesperson for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare said that federal officials did not provide details for why Idaho received less money in the second year of the program. “The program is in the process of reviewing the award and will be working with ( Centers for Medicare & Medicaid) to update the program’s workplan and budget,” spokesperson Greg Stahl said in an email. On Oct. 28, Idaho and federal authorities announced the state had awarded all of its first-year funds on projects such as infrastructure improvements at rural hospitals, emergency medical equipment, healthcare workforce development, mobile clinics and others. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid had been slated to announce the second-year grants on Oct. 31, but federal leaders told states on Oct. 30 that the announcement was delayed , KFF Health News reported. “This next $10 billion will expand access to care, strengthen the rural health workforce, improve prevention, and help states build solutions that fit the needs of their own communities,” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho, a Republican stronghold, the closest Democrat in this year’s election to securing a seat in Congress or statewide office was 11 points behind. The candidate, Ellie Gilbreath, was trying to stop Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson’s bid for reelection to a 15th term. Across the country last week, Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress , won governorships in most states and made headway in state legislatures . Amid national blue wave, Idaho Democrats gain six legislative seats — flipping competitive districts But by the time the national blue wave — or tsunami, as some are calling it — hit Idaho, the tide had turned it into a ripple. Idaho Democrats made modest gains. They swept full control of three legislative districts, gaining six more legislative seats , a shift that does little to chip away at Republicans’ supermajority control of the Legislature. And a closer look at election results shows that across the board, Democrats captured slightly more votes against Republican incumbents in statewide office and congress , who easily won reelection. But in all of those races, Democratic victory was still far off. No Democrat has won a statewide office in the state since 2002, and the last Democratic congressman in Idaho served in 2010. If Democrats want to upset decades of Idaho political history by winning a top of the ticket race, they have a long way to go. On average, Democrats gained 6 points of the vote share in federal and state races compared to the last time those offices were up for election. Still, Idaho Democrats this year were an average of 27 points behind Republicans, according to an analysis of election results by the Idaho Capital Sun. Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler wasn’t surprised that the blue wave didn’t carry Democrats through in Idaho. “Idaho is a solidly Republican state. We don’t tend to see too many competitive races” in the general election for statewide races, she said in an interview. “ … It’s just solid enough Republican that it’s hard for even a blue wave in other areas of the country to have too much influence, especially for those statewide races.” The Idaho Democratic Party also boasted another gain: Democrats got more of the vote in 67 legislative races than they did in 2024. This year’s election results are unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho, more than a third of votes in Tuesday’s election were cast before Election Day. Over 290,000 of the more than 731,000 ballots cast in the election were through early and absentee voting, according to data from the Idaho secretary of state’s office. That’s 100,000 more of those types of voting than were submitted during the state’s last election for statewide offices in 2022, according to the state election agency. Those forms of voting — available without a need to state a reason — allow voters to cast ballots either in person or by mail before Election Day. (Technically, some of these absentee ballots were submitted on Election Day. In Idaho, absentee ballots may be submitted until polls close at 8 p.m. local time on Election Day.) Democrats vote early and absentee at higher rates. Looking at state election data , the political makeup of the voters who cast ballots through early and absentee voting largely mirrors the state’s pool of more than 1 million registered voters , state data shows. With one caveat: Democrats vote early and absentee at higher rates. Here’s how it breaks down: About 59% of early and absentee voters this election were Republicans, which is slightly below the party affiliation of all registered voters, which is nearly 62% Republican. Unaffiliated voters make up nearly 22.3% of early and absentee voters, which is slightly lower than their nearly 24.6% share of Idaho’s total registered voters. Democrats make up nearly 18% of early and absentee voters. That’s a bigger rate of Idaho’s total registered Democrats, which is nearly 12%. Voters affiliated with third parties — the Constitution and Libertarian parties — make up a combined 0.76% of Idaho’s absentee voters. They make up less than 1.5% of all registered voters. There is also an age skew. Older voters, who make up most of Idaho’s total voters, vote early and absentee at higher rates than younger voters, the data show. Voters at least 45 years old make up 61.8% of the state’s registered voters, but cast 79% of the state’s early and absentee ballots this election. Voters age 44 and younger voted absentee and early less this year. They make up nearly 38.2% of registered voters, but just 21% of this year’s pre-Election Day votes. Voters aged 18 to 29 appeared the least likely to vote absentee and early this year. They cast only 7% of ballots early and absentee. But they make up 15.5% of registered voters, a higher share of the state’s overall voter pool than Idahoans age 75 and older, who make up nearly 13.8% of registered voters. It’s too early to tell how each of these demographics turned out to the polls this year. The secretary of state’s office hasn’t yet released more detailed information on the voters who showed up on Election Day. items.body: A video shows Idaho National Guard members approach Washington D.C. resident Anna King at her home in May. King has filed a $3 million claim against the Idaho National Guard. The U.S. Attorney's Office charged King with assault. (Screenshot from video) A Washington D.C. Superior Court judge has ordered the Idaho National Guard to produce documents related to an incident in May in which guards members detained a woman outside her home. D.C. resident Anna King filed a separate $3 million claim against the Idaho National Guard in July for injuries and distress she said she experienced when she was detained on May 8. Members of the Gem State’s National Guard have been in the nation’s Capital since February as part of a Joint Task Force, although there was no public announcement of the deployment until after King filed her claim, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Under the direction of D.C. Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro at a hearing Thursday, the Idaho National Guard, D.C. National Guard and U.S. Department of Defense will have to produce, or explain why they can’t produce, documents related to the detainment of King. King wrote in her tort claim against the Idaho National Guard that the troops did not explain why they were detaining her or provide a warrant when they approached her that evening. A video of the incident shows three men in National Guard uniforms approaching King, who had been sitting on a bench outside her apartment. King told the guards members not to touch her. She walked toward the steps to go back into her apartment, but the troops blocked her, the video showed. Two of them pinned her against the ground and secured her wrists behind her back. The U.S. government charged King with two counts of misdemeanor assault on a police officer on May 9. In August, the U.S. Attorney’s Office added three more charges of simple assault. The charges stem from alleged assaults on May 6. King pleaded not guilty and asked for a trial. King’s attorney, Jeffrey Nestler, said the Idaho National Guard provided one document, but the legal team felt it wasn’t sufficient. King’s attorneys asked for all reports, records, communications, directives and other documents from the Idaho National Guard related to King. Di Toro agreed, and ordered the prosecutor to ensure the entities produce relevant documents. According to court documents and Nestler, the Idaho National Guard members who detained King on May 8 said they had “prior run-ins” with King and had been ordered to detain her. “We’re here now in the part of the law that requires the government to do more than just ask questions, so I’m going to direct you to actually spend a little more time trying to understand whether prior to May 6, the Idaho National Guard had what the defense is calling a run-in with Ms. King,” Di Toro told Assistant United States Attorney Vanessa Jacobsen Thursday. As of Nov. 6, there are 27 Idaho National Guard troops in Washington D.C. There are more than 3,000 National Guard members from other states and territories. King is a former Army captain and Purple Heart and Bronze Star recipient, according to a press release announcing her tort claim. “As a trained combat veteran, I never imagined that armed National Guard members would attack, injure, and traumatize me at my home,” King said in the press release. “We are not at war with Americans, and my porch is not a war zone.” The trial in the case against King is scheduled to start July 27, 2027.
